$comment: The first assessment instrument (ADR-0030). Git was chosen because its semantics have not materially changed in a decade, its documentation is authoritative and citable, and the negative claim is easy to state honestly. Every item's answer follows from the linked git-scm.com page; none is copied from it. Curated, tier 3 — the same standing as the skill graph.

assessment.title: Git — documented behaviour of everyday commands
assessment.description: Ten questions about what Git commands do, as the official documentation defines them. Multiple choice, unproctored, and re-attemptable.
assessment.doesNotEvidence: Passing shows you can predict what these commands do. It does not show that you can recover a repository someone else broke, resolve a conflicted rebase under time pressure, design a branching strategy for a team, or diagnose a problem you have not seen before. It is unproctored and unattributed, so it also does not establish who sat it.

items.stem: You run `git reset --soft HEAD~1`. What happens to your staged changes and your working tree?

options.text: The commit is undone; its changes remain staged, and the working tree is untouched.
The commit is undone and its changes are discarded entirely.
The commit is undone; its changes are unstaged but kept in the working tree.
Nothing changes locally until you push.

items.evidences: Knows that --soft moves the branch pointer without touching the index or the working tree.

items.stem: A commit has already been pushed to a shared branch and turns out to be wrong. Which command undoes its effect without rewriting history other people have?

options.text: `git reset --hard` to the previous commit.
`git revert`, which records a new commit undoing the changes.
`git commit --amend`.
`git rebase -i` and dropping the commit.

items.evidences: Distinguishes undoing a change by adding a commit from undoing it by rewriting history.

items.stem: What does `git fetch` do that `git pull` does not stop at?

options.text: `git fetch` updates remote-tracking branches only; `git pull` also integrates the changes into the current branch.
`git fetch` downloads nothing until you specify a branch.
They are the same command; `pull` is an alias.
`git fetch` updates the working tree; `git pull` only updates refs.

items.evidences: Knows that fetching updates remote-tracking refs and does not change the current branch.

items.stem: A file is already tracked by Git. You add its path to `.gitignore`. What happens on the next commit?

options.text: The file is removed from the repository automatically.
Changes to it are still tracked and committed — .gitignore does not affect files already tracked.
Git refuses to commit until the conflict is resolved.
The file becomes untracked but stays on disk.

items.evidences: Knows that .gitignore governs untracked files, and that ignoring a tracked file requires removing it from the index.

items.stem: You rebase a local branch onto an updated main. What happens to the commits that were on your branch?

options.text: They keep their original hashes and are moved.
They are replaced by new commits with new hashes, applied on top of the new base.
They are merged into a single commit.
They are left untouched; only main moves.

items.evidences: Knows that rebasing creates new commits rather than relocating existing ones, which is why it rewrites history.

items.stem: Under what condition can Git complete a merge as a fast-forward?

options.text: When the two branches have no conflicting files.
When the current branch's commit is an ancestor of the branch being merged in.
Whenever `--no-ff` is not passed.
When both branches have the same number of commits.

items.evidences: Knows that a fast-forward requires the current tip to be an ancestor of the merged commit, so no merge commit is needed.

options.text: A new commit on the current branch introducing the changes from that commit.
A move of that commit from its branch to this one.
A merge commit joining the two branches.
A patch file you apply manually.

items.evidences: Knows that cherry-picking copies a commit's changes as a new commit rather than moving the original.

items.stem: You commit while in a detached HEAD state, then check out a branch without doing anything else. What is true of that commit?

options.text: It was discarded when you checked out the branch.
It exists but no branch or tag points at it, so it is reachable only by its hash until one does.
It was added to the branch you checked out.
It is staged but not yet committed.

items.evidences: Knows that commits made on a detached HEAD are real objects that become unreferenced when HEAD moves.

items.stem: Why is `git commit --amend` risky after the commit has been pushed?

options.text: It deletes the remote branch.
It replaces the commit with a new one, so the pushed commit and the local one diverge and a force push is needed.
It cannot be run once a commit is pushed.
It silently merges the remote version into yours.

items.evidences: Knows that amending creates a replacement commit rather than editing one in place.

items.stem: What does `git stash` do with your uncommitted changes?

options.text: Records them on a stack and reverts the working tree to the last commit, leaving no commit on any branch.
Creates a commit on the current branch.
Discards them permanently.
Pushes them to the remote as a draft.

items.evidences: Knows that stashing sets modifications aside without putting them on a branch, and that the working tree returns to HEAD.
